notes: Assignment to LICM was made by the programme on clinical grounds, and the groups differ sharply on almost everything that predicts employment. LICM participants were younger (42.6 versus 50.7 years), far more likely to have active psychotic symptoms (62.5% versus 21.4%), more likely to have a lifetime psychiatric admission (60.9% versus 22.7%) and an admission in the past year (17.5% versus 2.0%), more likely to have used illicit drugs (23.4% versus 6.8%), and much less likely to be employed at baseline (23.4% versus 48.9%). The authors state the selection rule explicitly: 'those with current severe symptoms, poor adherence to medication, problem behaviors ... and no or little support from family members were more likely to be selected for the programme'. Augmented inverse probability weighting on five covariates with the overlap assumption checked is a serious attempt to handle this, but symptom severity enters only as a binary indicator of current active psychosis, medication adherence is not measured at all, and the authors themselves concede that 'these results remain subject to residual confounding'.

source_locator: dissertation_shared_folder/Data Extraction Papers/individual-placement-and-support-for-vocational-recovery-in-first-episode-psychosis-randomised-controlled-trial.pdf; killackey2019, Method, Trial design, p. 76; Results, Baseline characteristics, p. 78; Table 1, p. 78; Table 2, p. 79
notes: Estimand: the effect of ASSIGNMENT to individual placement and support versus treatment as usual on being employed (at least one day of work at the legislated minimum wage) over the first 6 months. The same assessment attaches to both arm rows because RoB 2 appraises the randomised comparison they form. The sequence was computer-generated in random permuted blocks of four and eight at a 1:1 ratio by the study statistician, who was not associated with assessments or treatment and was the only person aware of the sequence, so generation and concealment are adequately described. Baseline differences are the concern: the groups differ significantly on sex (42.5% v. 19.2% female, chi-square 9.28, P = 0.002), depressive symptoms (P = 0.019), psychological and physical quality of life (P = 0.025 and 0.021) and time already spent in the EPPIC service (302 v. 216 days, P = 0.008), and baseline paid work, the outcome variable itself, differs at 21.9% v. 11.0% (P = 0.074). Chance imbalance is possible with n = 146, but the number and pattern of imbalances, all favouring neither arm consistently, warrant some concerns rather than low risk.

notes: Participants and clinicians were unmasked, but no differential deviations arising from participation in this trial are established. The workshops and clinical IPS-post conversion occurred in the two-year interval BEFORE this trial, following the earlier RCT, and describe background usual-care evolution rather than current-trial contamination. Excluding participants without observed outcomes belongs principally to the missing-data domain. These facts do not justify the original escalation above low for an assignment effect.

notes: Outcome data at 6 months are missing for 7 of 73 in the IPS arm (9.6%) and 13 of 73 in the TAU arm (17.8%), so the reported counts rest on 66 and 60 participants. Fifteen participants had no post-randomisation data at all and the imbalance is significant (TAU 16.4%, n = 12; IPS 4.1%, n = 3; chi-square 6.02, P = 0.014). Decisively, TWO of those participants 'withdrew participation as a result of having employment': missingness that depends directly on the true value of the outcome, in the direction of removing employed participants. No imputation was used for the reported rates, which are complete-case at 6 months. The authors' mitigation (no significant differences between those with and without data on baseline demographic, vocational and clinical variables) does not address outcome-dependent withdrawal.

notes: Employment was ascertained at interview by research assistants who were masked to allocation, who had no contact with the employment consultant, and participants were reminded at each assessment not to reveal whether they had been working with the employment consultant, so assessor blinding was actively maintained.
